rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an's denial that the devils are worthy of conveying revelation echoes the logic that a kingdom divided against itself cannot stand.
rows.anchor: Exactly the same point is made by the Qur’ ān by the words “neither is it worthy of them.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh could not produce anything like the Qur’an with their allies, showing that it was not from jinn or devils and that they lacked the capacity.
rows.anchor: they could not produce something like it. This obviously meant that the Qur’ ān was not the word of the jinn or the devils.

rows.speaker: The jinn
rows.claim: The jinn say that the heavens are now guarded, and an eavesdropper finds a meteor, supporting the claim that they can no longer hear revelation.
rows.anchor: but now whoever tries to eavesdrop finds a meteor waiting for him. (72:8-9)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The jinn passage points to God's arrangement to protect the Qur’an from every incursion by Satan and his army.
rows.anchor: an important arrangement made by God in His kingdom. It has been made by Him to protect the Qur’ ān

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although these and succeeding commands address the Prophet, their anger is directed at his opponents and rejecters.
rows.anchor: These and some of the succeeding are addressed to the Prophet (sws). However, the wrath and anger in them are directed to his opponents and rejecters.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet's greatest responsibility is to warn his near kin and show affection to believers who follow him.
rows.anchor: The Prophet (sws) is told that his greatest responsibility lies towards his near of kin.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet's immediate family custodied the House of God and were Arab religious and political leaders, so their position made warning them urgent.
rows.anchor: his immediate family who was the custodian of the House of God and also regarded by the Arabs to be their religious and political leaders.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Prophets first warn leaders because their acceptance can ease the message's spread; Jesus likewise focused on Jewish scholars before turning to the masses when they persisted in obduracy.
rows.anchor: the way prophets of God always adopted was that they warned the leaders of their time. They directed their attention to the masses

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lowering the wings of affection pictures a hen shielding her young from danger, expressing protective care for the believers who follow the Prophet.
rows.anchor: brings the picture of a hen protecting her young ones from danger lest they don’t realize it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Few of the Prophet's kin accepted his warning; the poor among the masses did, though Quraysh leaders considered them lowly, so he is told to warn one group and care for the other.
rows.anchor: Most of those who did were the poor among the masses whom the leaders of the Quraysh regarded to be very lowly in status.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If his kin disobey, the Prophet is to declare disassociation; this is the final warning phase, after which rejection brings messenger punishment and follower migration, as with Abraham before his father.
rows.anchor: This declaration of acquittal is the last phase of warning, as has been stated at other instances.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet should trust God through the coming hardships: God's might ensures none can stop His will, and His mercy will aid servants who forsake relatives for Him.
rows.anchor: Since He is powerful, He will be able to do what He intends. None can stop Him. And since He is merciful too

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The life phase after acquittal is unknown and arduous; turning friends into foes is difficult, and only trust in the powerful, merciful Lord carries them through.
rows.anchor: It is not at all easy to convert friends into foes when nothing is known of the future.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God watches the Prophet's night prayer and supplication, as well as his efforts to help companions share in its blessings, and will account for these deeds and aid him.
rows.anchor: The Prophet (sws) is also in God’s notice when he tries that his companions also reap the blessings of the night prayer and supplication.

rows.speaker: Exegetes
rows.claim: Exegetes offer various possible interpretations of “when you get up,” though the passage does not specify their alternatives.
rows.anchor: Out exegetes have presented various opinions in the interpretation of the expression “when you get up” and each can be possible.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author prefers reading the Prophet's getting up as rising for tahajjud, with the reference to his movement among prostrators providing a strong indication.
rows.anchor: in my opinion, the correct opinion among these is the one which says that this getting up relates to getting up for the tahajjud prayer.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The word translated as the Prophet's “coming and going” refers to his movement among those who prostrate.
rows.anchor: The word  means “coming and going.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet urged his companions to be diligent in night prayer and visited the mosque to see them praying; this extends his earlier charge to show affection by keeping followers spiritually vigilant.
rows.anchor: Earlier, in verse 215, he was directed to spread his wings of affection over the believers; this is another aspect of that directive

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Gospels similarly describe Jesus praying on a mountain during trial, urging disciples to stay awake, and repeatedly waking them to supplicate for protection.
rows.anchor: Jesus (sws) went to the mountains and busied himself in supplications and also asked his disciples to remain awake and pray to God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The attributes of hearing and knowing all are stated after the reference to night worship; remembering these attributes is integral to trusting God.
rows.anchor: Trusting God has a lot to do with keeping these attributes in mind.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After establishing the Qur’an's divine source, protected descent, and pure bearer, the passage answers the opponents' claim that devils inspired the Prophet with unseen knowledge as they do soothsayers.
rows.anchor: Earlier verses mention with full detail the source and fountainhead of the Qur’ān, its secure passage of descent and the purity of its bearer.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first trait, afāk, depicts soothsayers as outright liars, cheats, and swindlers who invent claims of revealed unseen knowledge to fool people.
rows.anchor: They are total liars, cheats and swindlers. In order to fool simpletons, they fabricate various lies

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The second trait, athīm, describes soothsayers as implicated in all kinds of moral sins.
rows.anchor: which means that they are incriminated with all sorts of moral sins.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Soothsayers stage meditation by chanting, then offer often meaningless rhymed prose as jinn-inspired revelation; the Qur’an calls this feigned listening samʿ, a practice used by many idolatrous religious figures to deceive people.
rows.anchor: these people enter into a state of meditation in which they chant words and then utter rhymed prose (which in most cases is meaningless).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some genuine sorcerers contact jinn and receive mixed true and false information, but most soothsayers are frauds; “most of them are liars” refers to the frauds, unlike a real magician who at least possesses an evil skill.
rows.anchor: Some among the soothsayers would know sorcery and make contact with the jinn from whom they would receive a mixture of right and wrong information.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Quraysh called the Qur’an poetry as propaganda against its growing proof of divine origin, attributing its eloquence to a human poet and jinn rather than an angelic revelation.
rows.anchor: when they saw that the eloquence of the Qur’ ān was conquering hearts and in this way its claim of being from God was being established day by day

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author proposes three benchmarks for distinguishing poetry from revelation and begins with the fact that misguided people follow poets; a work's followers reveal its character, unlike the upright followers of the messenger.
rows.anchor: The first benchmark put forth by the Qur’ ān is “and those who have gone astray follow the poets.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Poets held great sway over Arab masses, who followed their lead blindly; the Bakr–Taghlib feud lasted half a century after poet Muhalhal ibn Rabī‘ah ignited it.
rows.anchor: The famous scuffle between the Bakr and Taghlib tribes went on for half a century. A prominent poet Muhalhal ibn Rabī‘ah (d. 531 AD) was the one responsible in igniting this war.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The immorality of Arab poetry is illustrated by Imru’ al-Qays, whose lewd verse was unparalleled; despite being considered their greatest poet, Arabs called him the “wavered king.”
rows.anchor: He stands unparalleled in the lecherous content of his poetry. In spite of regarding him to be their greatest poet
